article.overview: A regolith electrostatic properties analyser is an instrument class for measuring how lunar regolith dust becomes electrically charged and how that charge moves dust near the surface. The sources reviewed for this article describe no flown, dedicated instrument with this exact function. The nearest examples are the flown Apollo 17 Surface Electrical Properties (SEP) experiment, which probed subsurface electrical properties with radio waves rather than measuring surface dust charge [4], and several development-stage instruments, including the Electrostatic Dust Analyzer (EDA), which its developers describe as reaching Technology Readiness Level 6 (TRL 6) but which has not been reported as flown [1][2].
article.description: The name covers instruments that could measure several linked quantities: the charge that builds up when dust contacts a material, the electric field near the surface, the electron and ion currents that supply charge, and, for dust that has been lofted, the charge, velocity, size and flux of individual grains [1][3]. These quantities are related but distinct, so an analyser may be designed for one of them or for a combination. The term is a descriptive working name rather than a standard instrument designation. The reviewed sources use names such as Electrostatic Dust Analyzer, Surface Electrical Properties experiment and electrostatic charging instrumentation.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: Electrostatic dust is treated in the reviewed sources as a crew-safety and equipment issue. The 2022 ICES paper reports that lunar regolith dust builds up charge and interacts electrostatically with rover wheels, astronaut boots and equipment, and gives improved dust mitigation as the goal of in-situ measurement [3]. The EDA paper states that its data will help assess crew safety and exploration-system risks, and may inform surface evolution on airless bodies [1]. The DUSTER project describes laboratory work on dust simulants as a way to understand regolith charging in space, paired with modelling [5]. The Apollo 17 SEP experiment had a different purpose: to detect electrical layering, discrete scattering bodies and possible water in the subsurface, and to obtain in-situ values of the dielectric constant and loss tangent of lunar material [4].
article.operating_principle:
Three measurement principles appear in the reviewed sources. The first is induced-charge sensing. In the EDA, two dust trajectory sensor units sit at opposite ends of the instrument, and each carries arrays of wire electrodes connected to charge-sensitive amplifiers. A charged grain passing through induces signals on the wires. These give the grain's total charge and a two-dimensional trajectory, and the time shift between the two sensor units gives its velocity [1].

The second principle is electrostatic deflection. A deflection field electrode between the two sensor units bends the grain's path. The deflection angle, combined with the measured charge, gives the charge-to-mass ratio and so the mass. The EDA analysis assumes a lunar dust density of about 3 g/cm3 to convert mass into size [1].

The third principle is field and plasma probing. The DUSTER concept proposes a Langmuir probe for electron temperature, electron density and plasma potential, an electric field probe, and a dust collector consisting of a high-voltage electrode coupled to an electrometer [5]. The ICES 2022 instrumentation is described as measuring the charge produced when regolith contacts space-rated materials, the electric field distribution near the surface and ion currents near the surface [3]. The Apollo 17 SEP experiment used a different principle, radio-frequency interferometry, in which electromagnetic waves are radiated into the ground and the interference pattern is analysed to infer subsurface electrical structure [4].
article.scientific_importance: Lunar dust charging and transport has been an open problem for more than five decades, according to the EDA paper [1]. Direct in-situ measurements of the charge, size, velocity and flux of lofted grains would test physical models of dust transport that are otherwise difficult to check on the surface. The ICES 2022 authors describe charging of dust in low gravity as non-intuitive because of interactions between individual grains, and they are developing a microgravity vacuum experiment to study it [3]. The sources link electrostatic dust to crew safety, equipment performance and surface evolution [1][3]. A single instrument would give measurements at one location, so its scientific value would depend on how many sites and conditions it sampled.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a regolith electrostatic properties analyser. The four examples below are a flown historical experiment with different measurement goals, a development-stage prototype with reported test data, and two concept-stage instruments described without hardware values. Their values are not comparable as a class, and no single mass, size or power figure should be taken as typical.

examples.name: Apollo 17 Surface Electrical Properties (SEP) experiment
examples.description: Type: historical lunar instrument, flown on Apollo 17 at Taurus-Littrow. The NTRS record of the 1973 Apollo 17 Preliminary Science Report describes the experiment as using electromagnetic radiation to explore subsurface material, with the purpose of detecting electrical layering, discrete scattering bodies and possible water, and obtaining the dielectric constant and loss tangent of lunar material in situ [4]. The record opened for this article does not state the transmitter and receiver configuration, frequencies, mass, dimensions or power [4]. A secondary search summary described a transmitter about 100 m from the Lunar Module, a receiver on the Lunar Roving Vehicle and frequencies from 1 to 32 MHz. These details were not verified against the full report, which could not be read in this run, and are not used as verified values. Mass, dimensions and power are therefore recorded as not verified.
examples.measurement_principle: Radio-frequency interferometry (subsurface electrical properties; not surface dust charge)
examples.transmitter_receiver_configuration: Not verified (full report not readable in this run)
examples.frequencies_mhz: Not verified (secondary summary listed 1-32 MHz; not confirmed)
examples.qualification: Flown on Apollo 17; mission-level qualification details not verified

examples.name: Electrostatic Dust Analyzer (EDA)
examples.type: Development-stage flight-qualified prototype (TRL 6 claimed; not reported as flown)
examples.description: Type: development-stage flight-qualified prototype, developed at the University of Colorado Boulder under NASA's DALI programme (project 18-DALI18_2-0025, principal investigator Xu Wang) [1][2]. The 2024 Planetary Science Journal paper calls it a high-fidelity and flight-qualified prototype that achieved TRL 6, and reports that it passed vibration and thermal-vacuum cycling tests. The paper does not state that the instrument has flown or been deployed on the Moon. Lunar measurements are described in the future tense [1]. The reported physical characteristics are a sensor module of 4.3 kg and a power consumption of 5 W. The overall dimensions are not stated in the paper text. Each wire electrode is 8 cm long and 0.5 mm in diameter. Each dust trajectory sensor unit has seven-wire arrays, and the instrument has 28 charge-sensitive amplifiers in total. The field of view is 135 degrees for flux measurement and 54 degrees for size measurement. The instrument can tilt through plus or minus 90 degrees in elevation, has electron-rejection grids at its entrances and reclosable doors, and the anti-Sun door opens to capture dust [1]. The digital signal processing module was outside the prototype's scope and ran on a desktop computer [1]. A secondary 2023 presentation summary gave different values (5.5 kg and 7.5 W); those figures are not used here because the primary paper gives 4.3 kg and 5 W.
examples.measurement_principle: Induced-charge sensing on wire electrodes with charge-sensitive amplifiers, plus electrostatic deflection for charge-to-mass ratio
examples.lab_tests: Vacuum 7 x 10^-7 Torr, JSC-1A simulant; see lab_performance_vs_requirements
examples.qualification: Prototype passed vibration and thermal-vacuum cycling per the 2024 paper; no flight reported

examples.name: Kennedy Space Center electrostatic charging instrumentation
examples.type: Concept (not named in the record opened)
examples.description: Type: concept described in a 2022 International Conference on Environmental Systems paper by authors at NASA Kennedy Space Center and the University of Central Florida. The instrument is not given a name in the record opened [3]. It is intended to measure in situ the charge produced when lunar dust contacts space-rated materials, the electric field distribution on or near the surface, and ion currents near the surface [3]. The mass, dimensions, power and flight status are not stated [3]. The same paper describes a planned microgravity vacuum experiment on dust charging in low gravity [3].
examples.measurement_principle: In-situ charge from dust contact with space-rated materials; electric field mapping; ion currents

examples.name: DUSTER in-situ dust-charging instrument
examples.type: Concept (prototype being designed and tested; no flight)
examples.description: Type: in-situ concept within the DUSTER project, led by the Royal Belgian Institute for Space Aeronomy (BIRA-IASB) with ONERA, the Instituto de Astrofisica de Andalucia (CSIC-IAA) and Thales Alenia Space Espana, and funded by the European Commission's Horizon Europe programme under grant agreement 101082466 [5]. The in-situ instrument would analyse the mechanical and electrical properties of dust and its electrostatic transport on a small lunar lander. It combines a Langmuir probe, an electric field probe and a dust collector [5]. The prototype is described as being designed, manufactured and tested in a controlled environment, with the aim of an engineering model. No lander, launch date, mass, size or power is given [5]. The laboratory work uses the DROP chamber at ONERA Toulouse, whose vacuum capability is not stated in the article [5].
examples.measurement_principle: Langmuir probe (electron temperature, density, plasma potential), electric field probe, dust collector with high-voltage electrode and electrometer

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No universal dimensions exist for a regolith electrostatic properties analyser. The only overall dimensions in the reviewed sources are the individual wire electrodes of the EDA, which are 8 cm long and 0.5 mm in diameter [1]. Overall dimensions are not stated for the EDA, the Apollo 17 SEP experiment, the ICES instrumentation or the DUSTER concept.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The EDA sensor module is reported as 4.3 kg [1]. No mass is verified for the Apollo 17 SEP experiment, the ICES instrumentation or the DUSTER concept in the sources reviewed. Mass should not be inferred across these examples, because the EDA figure refers to a sensor module and may not equal a complete flight unit.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: The EDA paper reports a power consumption of 5 W [1]. Power is not verified for the Apollo 17 SEP experiment, the ICES instrumentation or the DUSTER concept. The EDA digital signal processing module was outside the prototype's scope, so the paper's power figure does not include that module [1].

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: The reviewed sources point to vacuum, low gravity and thermal cycling as the main conditions a surface instrument must handle. The EDA prototype was tested for vibration, quasi-static loads and thermal-vacuum cycling, with the test values listed under Example 2 [1]. The ICES paper notes that charging in low gravity is not intuitive [3]. The operating environment of the Apollo 17 SEP experiment, including its thermal and power provisions, is not described in the record opened for this article [4].
article.limitations: A regolith electrostatic properties analyser has no confirmed flown, dedicated example in the sources reviewed. Most performance data for the EDA come from laboratory tests with JSC-1A simulant under vacuum, not from measurements of lunar regolith [1]. Electrostatic charging depends on regolith composition, particle size, surface history and the local plasma and photon environment, and simulant tests may not reproduce all of these. The EDA mass and power values come from one peer-reviewed paper, while a secondary presentation gives different values. The ICES and DUSTER sources give no performance figures. The Apollo 17 SEP experiment is a radio measurement of subsurface electrical properties, so it does not measure surface dust charge [4].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: The reviewed concepts are surface or lander instruments. The DALI programme has particular interest in small, stationary lander instruments [2], and the EDA and DUSTER concepts are described for lander use [1][5]. Integration would have to address dust exposure, because the instrument must collect or observe dust. The EDA paper describes reclosable doors and a tilt mechanism, and these would need mechanical, thermal and dust-protection interfaces confirmed for any host [1]. No specific lander, rover or spacecraft has been verified for any example.
transportation_process: Earth integration: the analyser and its sensor doors, power, data and thermal interfaces would be integrated into a lander or spacecraft payload. The reviewed sources do not specify these interfaces.
Launch and transfer: the instrument would be stowed for launch and transfer to the Moon. The reviewed sources do not describe launch-configuration constraints or door protection during launch.
Landing delivery: the instrument would be delivered to the surface by a lander whose identity is not yet verified for any example.

Deployment and setup: the instrument would be mounted with a clear view of the surface and sufficient clearance from the lander. The reviewed sources do not specify this viewing and clearance arrangement.

Power, data and commissioning: the EDA is described with a continuous measurement cadence [1]. Its digital signal processing module ran on a desktop computer in the prototype, so flight data handling would need an onboard processing design that the sources do not describe [1].
Operation: the concepts do not include sample return. Data would be relayed through the host spacecraft or lander, whose data interface is not verified.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: No deployment mechanism is specified in the reviewed sources for the EDA or DUSTER concepts. The EDA design includes a tilt mechanism of plus or minus 90 degrees in elevation and reclosable doors [1]. Any deployment would need to be defined by the host lander or rover, and no host has been verified.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Apollo 17 SEP experiment was set up on the lunar surface at Taurus-Littrow. The NTRS record reviewed does not describe its deployment [4]. A secondary search summary described crew transport and setup of the transmitter; this has not been verified against the full report.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a named lander, rover or spacecraft has been verified for any example. The DALI programme page lists the EDA as a lander or rover instrument without naming a host mission or launch date [2].

article.historical_significance: The Apollo 17 SEP experiment, flown in 1972, is the example in the reviewed sources most directly related to in-situ electrical measurements of the lunar surface [4]. It did not measure surface electrostatic charge, but it shows that electrical properties of lunar material have been studied in situ since the Apollo era [4]. A secondary 2023 conference summary describes the EDA as inherited from an earlier Electrostatic Lunar Dust Analyzer concept published in 2011. The original 2011 paper was not opened for this article, so that lineage is recorded as unverified. The EDA paper is the most detailed reviewed description of an in-situ electrostatic dust instrument with laboratory performance data [1].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The main uncertainty is that no regolith electrostatic properties analyser is confirmed as flown or as a dedicated lunar surface measurement. The EDA is described as TRL 6 and flight-qualified prototype in its paper, but the paper does not report a flight, and a secondary 2023 summary labels it an engineering model [1][2]. The EDA's mass and power conflict between sources, and its overall dimensions are not stated [1]. Its laboratory data use JSC-1A simulant under vacuum, and the flux accuracy method is not described [1]. For the Apollo 17 SEP experiment, the full report and the PDS instrument document could not be read in this run, so its antenna configuration, frequencies, mass, dimensions and power remain unverified [4]. The ICES and DUSTER sources give no numerical hardware values [3][5]. The reviewed material also includes conference abstracts and search summaries, so the evidence base is thinner than for a flown instrument. No lunar location or lander compatibility is asserted.

image_handling.url_policy: All URL values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. No image URLs were added because no image assets were verified for this draft. The DUSTER source page was read via its Europlanet web version, whose query string was removed; the cited PDF link is the canonical article location seen in search results and was not itself opened.

data_quality_notes: No images were researched or verified for this payload; payload.article.images, overview_images and all section-level image arrays are empty by design rather than omitted.

The Apollo 17 SEP PDS instrument document (a17l_sep.pdf) returned compressed, unreadable text, so its antenna configuration, frequencies, mass, dimensions and power could not be verified; the NTRS record opened does not state them either.

EDA mass and power are taken from the 2024 Planetary Science Journal paper (4.3 kg sensor module, 5 W). A secondary 2023 presentation summary gives 5.5 kg and 7.5 W; the conflict is recorded and the primary figures are used.

The EDA overall dimensions are not stated in the paper text. The paper describes the instrument as flight-qualified and TRL 6, but it does not report a flight, and a secondary summary labels it an engineering model.
The EDA flux accuracy (20 per cent) is listed in the paper's requirements table, but the paper does not describe how it was tested.

The DUSTER article's laboratory description was checked against the article text; it describes the DROP chamber at ONERA Toulouse and does not mention a Kelvin probe, VUV lamp or Faraday cup, which appear in a search summary but not in the article.
The 2011 Electrostatic Lunar Dust Analyzer (ELDA) precursor is mentioned only through a secondary 2023 summary; the original paper was not opened and its author list was not verified.
The Apollo 17 SEP transmitter/receiver layout and frequency range come from a secondary search summary and are not used as verified values.
The KSC instrumentation is not named in the source record opened, and the record does not state limitations or hardware values.
